title: Headphone impedance and sensitivity explained: do you need an amp?
metaDescription: What ohms and decibel sensitivity figures mean on headphones, why some sound quiet from a phone, and when a headphone amplifier or USB DAC helps.
excerpt: Some wired headphones sound quiet and thin plugged into a phone. Impedance and sensitivity explain why, and when an amplifier is worth buying.
_note: AI-assisted draft from public sources. Check every fact, add your own experience and photos, then publish from /studio.
answer: Impedance, in ohms, tells you how much the headphones resist the electrical signal; sensitivity tells you how loud they get for a given input. Low-impedance, high-sensitivity headphones are easy to drive from phones and laptops. High-impedance or low-sensitivity models may need a headphone amplifier to reach a comfortable volume with good control.

sections.heading: Impedance
sections.body:
Impedance is the electrical resistance a headphone presents to the device driving it, measured in ohms. Most portable headphones and earbuds sit between about 16 and 64 ohms. Many studio and hi-fi headphones are 80, 250, 300 ohms or more.

Higher impedance on its own is not better or worse. It changes how much voltage is needed to reach a given volume. A phone's headphone output produces limited voltage, so it can struggle to drive high-impedance headphones loud enough.

sections.heading: Sensitivity
sections.body:
Sensitivity, sometimes called efficiency, tells you how loud a headphone plays for a given input. It is quoted in decibels, either per milliwatt (dB/mW) or per volt (dB/V). The two are not directly comparable, which makes spec sheets confusing.

Higher sensitivity means louder for the same signal. A low-impedance, high-sensitivity earphone gets loud from almost anything, sometimes too easily, revealing background hiss from a poor source. A high-impedance, low-sensitivity headphone needs a stronger signal.

sections.heading: When a phone or laptop is not enough
sections.body:
Signs your source is struggling:

- You need maximum volume or close to it for normal listening.
- Bass sounds weak or loose, and the sound becomes harsh at higher volumes.
- The volume is fine on quiet recordings but loud passages distort.

Many phones no longer have a headphone socket at all, and the small USB-C or Lightning adaptors that replace it vary widely in power. Some are fine for earbuds but underpowered for larger headphones.

sections.heading: DACs and amplifiers
sections.body:
Digital music has to be converted to an analogue signal by a DAC (digital-to-analogue converter) and then amplified to drive the headphones. Phones and laptops do both internally.

An external USB DAC with a built-in amplifier, from small dongle-style devices to desktop boxes, can provide more power, a lower noise floor and better control of demanding headphones. For most earbuds and portable headphones, it makes little audible difference. For high-impedance studio headphones or planar magnetic headphones with low sensitivity, it can be transformative.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
sections.body:
- **Wireless headphones** have their own built-in DAC and amplifier, so impedance does not matter for them.
- **Earbuds and portable wired headphones** are designed to work from phones without help.
- **Studio and hi-fi headphones** above about 80 ohms, or planar models with low sensitivity, often benefit from a dedicated amplifier.
- **Check the maker's guidance;** many state whether an amplifier is recommended.
- **Mind the volume.** More power means more capacity to damage your hearing. Start low.

faq.q: Do 250 ohm headphones need an amp?
faq.a: Usually, yes, for comfortable volume and good control. Phones and many laptops cannot provide enough voltage.

faq.q: Does a USB DAC improve sound quality?
faq.a: With easy-to-drive earbuds the difference is often small. It helps most with demanding headphones or a noisy built-in output.
